pageTitle: Morphology of brood pouch formation in the pot-bellied seahorse Hippocampus abdominalis
quote: Embryos are finally embedded within individual compartments formed in pseudoplacenta [11], and there, the number of blood vessels increases. The brood pouch, like the mammalian placenta, performs the functions of gas exchange, waste removal, and osmoregulation [9, 12-14]. ... The epithelium facing the lumen of the pouch is considered to be derived from epithelium that covers the outser surface of the body.
unsupported: "The pouch seals shut"; "and feeding"; "a mammal's placenta grows from embryonic tissue". The paper calls the tissue a pseudoplacenta and says its skin origin is "considered", not proven.
correctedFact: The male seahorse does more than carry eggs. Inside his brood pouch the embryos become embedded in individual compartments of a blood-rich lining that, like a mammal's placenta, handles gas exchange, waste removal and salt balance. That lining is thought to come from the same epithelium that covers the outside of his body.
note: The paper lists waste removal and osmoregulation, not feeding, as the placenta-like functions.

pageTitle: Gene loss and co-option of toll-like receptors facilitate paternal immunological adaptation in the brood pouch of pregnant male seahorses
quote: In this study, comparative genomic analysis revealed that all syngnathid species lost three vertebrate-conserved Toll-like receptors (TLR1, TLR2, and TLR9), of which all play essential roles in immune protection and immune tolerance in the uterus and placenta during pregnancy. ... with the loss of several MHC II pathway genes in the pipefishes and a highly divergent invariant chain (CD74) in seahorses (14).
unsupported: "they lost their spleen" (not in this paper); "A vertebrate missing all that should be defenseless" (the paper says other TLRs partly compensate).
correctedFact: Carrying young means carrying tissue the immune system could read as foreign. Seahorses and their relatives answered by losing immune hardware: every syngnathid lacks TLR1, TLR2 and TLR9, three Toll-like receptors other vertebrates kept, and their MHC II pathway is lost in pipefishes and heavily altered in seahorses.
note: Spleen loss is reported separately in Nature Communications (2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9734139/ : "a specific amino-acid replacement in the tlx1 transcription factor is associated with seahorses' asplenia (loss of spleen...)". That paper does not cover the TLRs, so no single page carries all three claims.

pageTitle: Hepcidin Gene Co-Option Balancing Paternal Immune Protection and Male Pregnancy
quote: The closed brood pouch of seahorse provides the ideal conditions for bacterial proliferation (filled with non-sterile seawater and the nutrient-rich pouch fluid), therefore, it is essential to balance the paternal immune molecules and commensal microbiota and maintain a pathogen-limited environment in seahorse brood pouches during pregnancy. ... The expression of HehampII genes in the brood pouch placenta (A) of lined seahorse (Hippocampus erectus) was higher during pregnancy
unsupported: "lysozyme"; "When a female transfers her eggs, non-sterile seawater goes into the pouch with them" (the paper says the pouch is filled with seawater, not when it enters); "warm"; "handling bacteria the missing immune hardware no longer can".
correctedFact: A pregnant seahorse's closed brood pouch is filled with non-sterile seawater and nutrient-rich fluid, ideal conditions for bacteria. Part of the defense is chemical: seahorse hepcidin genes, which make antimicrobial peptides, are expressed more strongly in the pouch lining during pregnancy, and the peptides clump bacteria and neutralize their toxins.
note: Lysozyme appears in the paper only as a gene family searched for, not as one running high in the pouch.

pageTitle: A Snapshot-Based Mechanism for Celestial Orientation
quote: In order to protect their food from competitors, ball-rolling dung beetles detach a piece of dung from a pile, shape it into a ball, and roll it away along a straight path. ... Instead, they appear to form an internal representation of the prevailing celestial scene, a "celestial snapshot," ... This happens during the "dance," a behavior in which the beetle climbs on top of its ball and rotates about its vertical axis.
unsupported: "It has no destination and no idea which way it is going".
correctedFact: Before rolling, a dung beetle climbs on top of its ball and turns in place. That dance is a reading: the beetle takes a snapshot of the celestial cues overhead, then holds its bearing to them so it can roll the ball away from rivals at the dung pile along a straight line.
note: Abstract only (PubMed); DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2016.03.030.

pageTitle: Dung Beetles Watch the Galaxy (That's How They Roll)
quote: Since each beetle rolls at a constant speed, Dacke and Warrant could measure how far they had travelled by marking the time between their entrance into the arena and the sound of their exit. Under a full moon, they took 21 seconds. Under a moonless, starry night, their paths wavered more and they took 40 seconds. On a cloudy night, or if Dacke and Warrant covered their heads with a black cap (...), the beetles took around 120 seconds to reach the edge.
unsupported: "two meter arena"; "With the Milky Way visible" (the source says a moonless, starry night); "That gap is also what light pollution costs an animal, measured directly".
correctedFact: Researchers timed dung beetles rolling from the center of a walled arena to its edge. Under a moonless, starry sky they took about 40 seconds. On a cloudy night, or wearing a cap that hid the sky, the same trip took around 120 seconds, and since beetles roll at a steady speed, the extra time is extra wandering.
extraPoints: Light pollution: the card reads the timing gap as a direct measure of what light pollution costs, which the source does not say.
note: Under a full moon the beetles were faster still (21 seconds), so the starry-sky time is not the best case.

pageTitle: Dung Beetles Watch the Galaxy (That's How They Roll)
quote: The beetle's eyes are not sensitive enough to pick out individual stars but it can see the Milky Way as a fuzzy stripe, streaking across the night sky. ... So they took their beetles and arenas to the planetarium at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. If they projected the bright stripe of the Milky Way onto the building's 18-metre domed ceiling, the beetles could find their way out of the arena reasonably quickly. It didn't matter whether the team added another 4,000 stars - it was the Milky Way that mattered. If they left out this galactic stripe, or only added the 18 brightest stars, the beetles took much longer to find their way out.
unsupported: "they fell apart" (the source says they took much longer).
correctedFact: To prove which part of the sky mattered, researchers took beetles into a Johannesburg planetarium. With only the Milky Way projected they found their way out quickly, and adding 4,000 stars changed nothing. With only the brightest stars and no Milky Way, they took much longer. Their eyes cannot pick out single stars.
note: Only the strength of "fell apart" is off; everything else matches. The dash in the quote is a hyphen standing in for the source's dash.

pageTitle: Epidermal threads reveal the origin of hagfish slime
quote: A single pinch on the tail of an adult Pacific hagfish (Eptatretus stoutii; ~45 cm body length) can cause the production of 0.9 l of slime, which is ~7 times the volume of the animal (~0.14 l) (Fudge et al., 2005). ... The slime deploys in less than half a second, exuding from specialized glands on the hagfish's body and expanding up to 10,000 times its ejected volume. The defensive slime is highly dilute, consisting mostly of sea water ... Within 400 ms after ejection, coiled threads from GTCs unravel and mucous vesicles from gland mucous cells swell and deform, resulting in a network of mucus and threads that entraps large volumes of water
note: The 0.9 L figure originates in Fudge et al. (2005), cited by this paper.

publisher: Journal of Venomous Animals and Toxins including Tropical Diseases (2013)
pageTitle: Mad, bad and dangerous to know: the biochemistry, ecology and evolution of slow loris venom
quote: The venom is usually delivered after a threatened loris raises it arms above its head, combining fluid of its brachial gland (Figure 1) with saliva [7]. In this classic defence posture (Figure 2), the mouth can quickly be moved to the brachial gland to combine the fluids, and the mixture applied to the top of the head for defence or kept in the mouth to bite [8]. ... Alterman discovered that loris venom was only deadly when secretions from a loris' brachial gland (brachial gland exudates - BGE) were combined with saliva. ... Venom is activated by combining the oil from the brachial arm gland with saliva
note: The paper places the gland "on the inside of the elbow region"; the card says upper arm, which is close enough for a brachial gland. "Harmless alone" rests on the mouse experiments, where the secretion was deadly only with saliva.

publisher: Journal of Venomous Animals and Toxins including Tropical Diseases (2013)
pageTitle: Mad, bad and dangerous to know: the biochemistry, ecology and evolution of slow loris venom
quote: Research on a handful of captive samples from three of eight slow loris species reveals that the protein within slow loris venom resembles the disulphide-bridged heterodimeric structure of Fel-d1, more commonly known as cat allergen. ... They interpreted the propensity of only some individuals to suffer anaphylaxis from loris bites as consistent with variable sensitivity to a protein allergen.
unsupported: "behind most human cat allergies"; "less a toxin evolved to attack nerves or blood"; "Much of the damage is done by the victim's own immune response" (the paper only links anaphylaxis in some people to allergen sensitivity).
correctedFact: The main protein in slow loris venom resembles Fel d 1, the cat allergen, sharing its disulphide-bridged heterodimeric structure. That may explain why only some people bitten by a slow loris go into anaphylactic shock: as with a cat allergy, the reaction seems to depend on how sensitive the victim is.

pageTitle: Tickled to Death: Analysing Public Perceptions of 'Cute' Videos of Threatened Species (Slow Lorises - Nycticebus spp.) on Web 2.0 Sites
quote: Illegally-traded animals routinely have their anterior teeth inhumanely clipped out by vendors, a practice that inhibits release of animals back to the wild and often results in their death [21], [22]. ... At International Animal Rescue in Indonesia, of 180 confiscated lorises from Java Sumatra and Borneo from 2008-2011, 64% had their teeth removed, eliminating any hope for reintroduction.
unsupported: "nail clippers or pliers" (pliers appear only in a quoted YouTube comment); "without anesthetic"; "Infection and blood loss kill many before they reach a buyer"; "cannot eat its natural diet or defend itself".
correctedFact: Slow lorises sold illegally as pets routinely have their front teeth clipped out by vendors, a practice that often kills them. Survivors pay for life: at one Indonesian rescue center, 64 percent of 180 confiscated lorises had lost their teeth this way, ending any hope of returning them to the wild.
note: The motive (stopping bites to buyers) is in the Batch K venom review, PMC3852360: "Indonesian pet traders who routinely cut out the lorises' front teeth to prevent their biting potential purchasers".

pageTitle: The chicken that lived for 18 months without a head
quote: "You'd be amazed how little brain there is in the front of the head of a chicken," says Smulders. It is mostly concentrated at the back of the skull, behind the eyes, he explains. Reports indicate that Mike's beak, face, eyes and an ear were removed with the hatchet blow. But Smulders estimates that up to 80% of his brain by mass ... remained untouched. ... a timely blood clot luckily prevented him bleeding to death.
unsupported: "The brain stem sits low ... angled into the neck"; "most of the skull"; "It also missed the jugular".
correctedFact: Mike the Headless Chicken survived because a chicken's brain is not where you would guess. It sits mostly at the back of the skull, behind the eyes, so the hatchet took his beak, face and eyes but left up to 80 percent of his brain. A timely blood clot stopped him bleeding to death.
note: Sources disagree on the jugular: History Colorado (cached F_chicken_hc) says a clot formed "in Mike's severed jugular", the opposite of "missed the jugular". The BBC also notes that most of what was then called the brain stem is now counted as brain proper.

pageTitle: The chicken that lived for 18 months without a head
quote: Mike was fed with liquid food and water that the Olsens dropped directly into his oesophagus. Another vital bodily function they helped with was clearing mucus from his throat. They fed him with a dropper, and cleared his throat with a syringe. The night Mike died, they were woken in their motel room by the sound of the bird choking. When they looked for the syringe they realised they had left it at the sideshow, and before they could find an alternative, Mike suffocated.
unsupported: "On 17 March 1947" (the source says spring 1947); "hotel" (the source says motel).
correctedFact: With no beak, Mike was fed liquid food by dropper straight into his esophagus, and his owners cleared mucus from his throat with a syringe. In spring 1947, in a Phoenix motel room while on tour, he began choking in the night. The syringe had been left at the sideshow, and he suffocated.
note: The source places the death in Phoenix in "the spring of 1947".

pageTitle: The chicken that lived for 18 months without a head
quote: Beheading disconnects the brain from the rest of the body, but for a short period the spinal cord circuits still have residual oxygen. Without input from the brain these circuits start spontaneously. "The neurons become active, the legs start moving," says Dr Tom Smulders of Newcastle University. Usually the chicken is lying down when this happens, but in rare cases, neurons will fire a motor programme of running. "The chicken will indeed run for a little while," says Smulders. "But not for 18 months, more like 15 minutes or so."
unsupported: "in the brain stem" (the source names spinal cord circuits); "flap"; "Mike was that ordinary phenomenon stretched to 18 months"; "including walking and balancing, was never consciously driven".
correctedFact: Running around like a headless chicken describes something real. Beheading cuts the brain off from the body, but spinal cord circuits still hold some oxygen and, with no input from above, start firing on their own. Usually only the legs move, but sometimes the bird really runs, for perhaps 15 minutes.
note: The BBC explains Mike differently: most of his brain survived the blow, so he was not the reflex phenomenon stretched out. The card's framing contradicts the source.

pageTitle: Meowing and Yowling
quote: Meowing is an interesting vocalization in that adult cats don't actually meow at each other, just at people. Kittens meow to let their mother know they're cold or hungry, but once they get a bit older, cats no longer meow to other cats. But they continue to meow to people throughout their lives, probably because meowing gets people to do what they want.
unsupported: "wild cats grow out of"; "Adult cats living together for years"; "relying on scent and body language instead".
correctedFact: Meowing starts as a kitten's call to its mother when it is cold or hungry. Once cats grow up they stop meowing at other cats, yet they keep meowing at people throughout their lives, probably because the sound gets people to do what they want.

pageTitle: Cats manipulate their owners with a cry embedded in a purr
quote: On the surface, the "solicitation purrs" are based on the same low-pitched sounds that contented moggies make, but embedded within them is a high-pitched signal that sounds like a cry or a meow. ... Her volunteers rated the purrs of a food-seeking cat to be more urgent and less pleasant than purrs made while resting, sitting or petting. ... They could do so even if they had never owned a cat before ... At a frequency of around 380 Hz (middle G or thereabouts), this extra sound stood out from the typical low frequencies of a purr, and is more like a cry or a meow. The frequency is actually very similar to that of a crying infant
unsupported: "without being told which is which" (implied by the playback test, not stated); "harder to ignore" (the source says less pleasant).
correctedFact: Cats asking for food produce a variant researchers call the solicitation purr, with a high-pitched component around 380 Hz buried inside the normal low rumble, close to the pitch of a crying infant. Listeners rate these purrs as more urgent and less pleasant than ordinary purring, even people who have never owned a cat.
note: Study: McComb et al., Current Biology (2009). Near confirmed; the gaps are wording.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
pageTitle: Lion
quote: Lions are the world's most social felines. They live in groups of related females, called prides ... Females usually stay in their mothers' prides for life, unless food scarcity forces them out. ... They create coalitions, usually with brothers and cousins, and search for a pride to take over. ... Adult males that are fortunate enough to achieve residency within a pride hold tenure for an average of two years, often leaving due to eviction by another coalition of males. ... In the wild, a lioness may live up to 16 years
unsupported: "the only social cat out of roughly forty species" (the source says most social).
correctedFact: Lions are the world's most social cats, and the pride is built on related females who usually stay in their mothers' prides for life. Males are not part of that lineage. They arrive as a coalition, hold the pride for about two years on average, and are often evicted by another coalition.

pageTitle: How Lions Became Social
quote: An early idea was that groups had better success at hunting. "Craig and a graduate student found that females could eat fine alone, taking wildebeest and anything smaller," says Mosser. "But hunting success dropped in groups of about two to four females, then rose as groups got bigger." ... The best territories were near the confluences of streams, where water was plentiful and dense vegetation offered shade, a place to hide the cubs and cover for stalking. "We tested this by looking where kills occurred near confluences. Many happened inside the 'V' where streams come together," she says. Was territorial defense the reason for grouping? It appeared to be; larger prides had better territories.
unsupported: "food per lion does not reliably improve with group size, because a kill split more ways feeds each one less"; "where prey must come to drink".
correctedFact: The obvious explanation for lion prides is cooperative hunting, but decades of Serengeti research do not back it: females eat fine alone, and hunting success actually dips in groups of two to four. What pride size does track is territory quality. Larger prides hold the best ground, near river confluences where kills cluster.
note: Research by Anna Mosser and Craig Packer on Serengeti prides.

unsupported: All of it: the 14 Hz floor, hearing only the upper harmonics, the carrying distance, dusk temperature inversions and the calling peak.
extraPoints: Dusk temperature inversions channel the sound and calling activity peaks then.
note: Cornell Elephant Listening Project pages (the likely source) return 403 to this sandbox; Larom et al. 1997 is not indexed on PubMed or PMC. Search snippets suggest ELP does describe evening inversions, so a desktop check of https://www.birds.cornell.edu/ccb/elephant-listening-project/sound/ may confirm it.

pageTitle: The distribution, density and three-dimensional histomorphology of Pacinian corpuscles in the foot of the Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) and their potential role in seismic communication
quote: Both African and Asian elephant high-amplitude low-frequency vocalizations in the range of 20-40 Hz travel through the air as acoustic waves and also propagate through the ground as seismic waves ... Behaviors exhibited in response to seismic signals include ceasing normal activity to adopt a motionless, 'freezing' posture, scanning the horizon, orienting toward the source of the seismic signal (Fig. 6A), shifting weight to the forefeet, lifting 1 foot to touch the most anterior portion of the foot to the ground ... Proposed pathways for elephant detection of these vibrations include bone conduction, somatosensory reception or both.
unsupported: "as a surface wave that outruns the airborne version" (the paper says seismic signals "travel at different rates"); "up the leg to the middle ear" (the paper names bone conduction only as a proposed pathway).
correctedFact: A loud elephant rumble does not only move air, it also travels through the ground as seismic waves. Elephant feet hold clusters of Pacinian corpuscles, the receptors mammals use to sense vibration. Played rumbles through the ground, elephants freeze, shift their weight forward and lift one foot to touch its tip down.
note: Corpuscle anatomy is from Asian elephants; the playback behavior is from African elephants in Etosha.

pageTitle: Study: Swarm bees use 'stop' signals to make decisions, as do brain neurons
quote: scout bees also use inhibitory "stop signals" -- a short buzz delivered with a head butt to the dancer -- to inhibit the waggle dances produced by scouts advertising competing sites. The strength of the inhibition produced by each group of scouts is proportional to the group's size. This inhibitory signaling helps ensure that only one of the sites is chosen. ... Seeley and colleagues found that scouts that had committed to one box directed their stop signals mainly toward scouts promoting the other box.
unsupported: "around 350 Hz"; "Enough of these and the rival dancer stops" (the source says the signals inhibit dancing).
correctedFact: When a swarm is choosing a new home, scout bees advertise sites by dancing. Scouts committed to one site also deliver stop signals, a short buzz delivered with a head butt, aimed mainly at bees dancing for a rival site. The inhibition grows with each group's size and helps ensure only one site wins.
note: Study: Seeley et al., Science (December 2011).

pageTitle: How 10,000 bees decide where to go when they fly the coop -- decision-making to rival any department committee
quote: As soon as 15 or more bees are at any one site, the researchers found, the scouts signal to the waiting bees in the swarm that it's time to warm up their flight muscles in preparation for takeoff. ... To test whether the bees decide by quorum or consensus ... As soon as about 15 bees were seen at one site, the swarm would take off for it, even though some scouts were still dancing strongly for the other site. ... the researchers offered swarms four small and one superior site in size. Although the superior site was never the first one found, it was almost always chosen.
unsupported: "fifteen to twenty" (the source says about 15); "about 80 percent of the time" (the source says almost always); "The queen does not participate".
correctedFact: A swarm never tallies a vote. Once about 15 scouts are at one candidate cavity at the same time, they signal the waiting swarm to warm its flight muscles for takeoff, even while others still dance for rival sites. Offered one superior nest box among four small ones, swarms almost always chose the best.
extraPoints: How often swarms pick the best site (the card's 80 percent figure).
note: Same publisher and page used for a bee fact in Batch B.

pageTitle: Are penguins really monogamous?
quote: "The short answer is no, penguins are not really monogamous," said Emma Marks ... a 1999 study in the journal The Auk found that only 15% of emperor penguins (Aptenodytes forsteri) seek out the same partner for subsequent breeding seasons. Most species return to the same partners at least somewhat consistently, with fidelity rates between 59% and 89%, according to the 2013 study.
unsupported: "Gentoos, by contrast, can exceed 90 percent"; "The difference is ... whether the species builds a nest: a fixed spot gives two birds somewhere to find each other again".
correctedFact: The lifelong penguin romance is mostly myth. Emperor penguins seek out the same partner in a later breeding season only about 15 percent of the time, and even the more faithful species fall short of perfect: across most penguins, mate fidelity runs between roughly 59 and 89 percent.
note: The original Auk (1999) paper was unreachable: its SORA PDF now redirects to a landing page.

pageTitle: Emperor penguin
quote: But only the males take on the incubation duties. ... Emperor colonies also face blizzards of up to 200 km/h. To keep warm, the males close ranks to share their warmth. ... Huddling cuts the heat loss by as much as 50%, and enables males to survive the long incubation fast. ... On windy days, those on the windward edge feel the cold more than those in the centre and down-wind. One-by-one they peel off the mob and shuffle, egg on feet, down the flanks of the huddle to join it again on the leeward side.
unsupported: "below minus 40 Celsius"; "for roughly 65 days"; "can lose close to half his body weight"; "to the middle" (the source has birds rejoining on the leeward side and passing through the warm center).
correctedFact: Only male emperor penguins incubate, balancing the egg on their feet through the Antarctic winter while fasting, in blizzards that reach 200 km/h (about 124 mph). Huddling cuts their heat loss by as much as half, and the huddle keeps moving: birds on the windward edge shuffle down its flanks to rejoin on the sheltered side.
extraPoints: Huddle rotation is a separate point from the fast and weight loss.
note: A second page (NSF, Emperors of the Antarctic) returned 404.

pageTitle: 'Crocs' exhibit opening May 18 features live reptiles
quote: "More closely related to birds and dinosaurs than other living reptiles, the crocodilians in this exhibit provide a window into the unique biology and conservation challenges of these fantastic animals." (David Blackburn, Florida Museum associate curator of herpetology)
unsupported: "archosaurs" (term not used); "They are dinosaur relatives that lived while their cousins did not".
correctedFact: Crocodilians look like oversized lizards, but on the family tree they sit closer to birds and dinosaurs than to any other living reptile, lizards included. The likeness to lizards is body plan, not ancestry: a crocodile is a closer relative of a sparrow than of a monitor lizard.

pageTitle: Curious Kids: how did crocodiles survive the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs?
quote: Firstly, crocodile bodies use very little energy. They lie around a lot, breathe slowly and even have a very slow heartbeat. ... It also means they can go without food for months, and sometimes more than a year. This would have been very helpful when food (such as other animals) became hard to find once the asteroid hit. ... But the crocodile survivors mostly lived in places like rivers, lakes and coasts. The animals living in these places don't need green plants as much. Dead plants and animal material washes in from surrounding land, which is eaten by tiny creatures, which are then eaten by larger creatures including crocodiles.
unsupported: "Being ectothermic cuts food needs roughly tenfold against a mammal the same size"; "fresh water" (the source says rivers, lakes and coasts).
correctedFact: Crocodiles came through the asteroid impact that ended the dinosaurs by needing so little. Their bodies use very little energy, so they can go months without food. And they lived in rivers, lakes and coasts, where food webs run on dead material washing in from the land, so losing green plants mattered less.
note: Written by Flinders University evolutionary biologist Michael Lee.
